11. And such were ye. Some add a term of speciality: Such were some of you, as in Greek the word τινὲς is added; but I am rather of opinion that the Apostle speaks in a general way. I consider that term to be redundant, in accordance with the practice of the Greeks, who frequently make use of it for the sake of ornament, not by way of restriction. We must not, however, understand him as putting all in one bundle, so as to attribute all these vices to each of them, but he simply means to intimate, that no one is altogether free from these vices, until he has been renewed by the Spirit. For we must hold this, that man’s nature universally contains the seed of all evils, but that some vices prevail and discover themselves more in some than in others, according as the Lord brings out to view the depravity of the flesh by its fruits.
Thus Paul, in the first chapter of his Epistle to the Romans, piles up many different kinds of vices and crimes, which flow from ignorance of God, and that ingratitude, of which he had shown all unbelievers to be guilty, (Romans 1:21-32) — not that every unbeliever is infected with all these vices, but that all are liable to them, and no one is exempt from them all. For he who is not an adulterer, sins in some other way. So also in the third chapter he brings forward as applicable to the sons of Adam universally those declarations —
their throat is an open sepulcher: their feet are swift to shed blood: their tongue is deceitful or poisonous, (Romans 3:13-15)
— not that all are sanguinary and cruel, or that all are treacherous or revilers; but that, previously to our being formed anew by God, one is inclined to cruelty, another to treachery, another to impurity, another to deceit; so that there is no one in whom there does not exist some trace of the corruption common to all; and we are all of us, to a man, by an internal and secret affection of the mind, liable to all diseases, unless in so far as the Lord inwardly restrains them from breaking forth openly.
“Suiets a toutes sortes de vices, sinon entant que le Seigneur les reprime au dedans, afin qu’ils ne sortent dehors, et vienent “a estre mis en effet;” — “Liable to all kinds of vices, unless in so far as the Lord inwardly restrains them, that they may not break forth outwardly, and come to be put in practice.”
The simple meaning, therefore, is this, that prior to their being regenerated by grace, some of the Corinthians were covetous, others adulterers, others extortioners, others effeminate, others revilers, but now, being made free by Christ, they were such no longer.
The design of the Apostle, however, is to humble them, by calling to their remembrance their former condition; and, farther, to stir them up to acknowledge the grace of God towards them. For the greater the misery is acknowledged to be, from which we have escaped through the Lord’s kindness, so much the more does the magnitude of his grace shine forth. Now the commendation of grace is a fountain
“Vne fontnine abondante;” — “An abundant fountain.”
of exhortations, because we ought to take diligent heed, that we may not make void the kindness of God, which ought to be so highly esteemed. It is as though he had said: “It is enough that God has drawn you out of that mire in which you were formerly sunk;” as Peter also says,
“The time past is sufficient to have fulfilled the lusts of the Gentiles.” (1 Peter 4:3.)
But ye are washed He makes use of three terms to express one and the same thing, that he may the more effectually deter them from rolling back into the condition from which they had escaped. Hence, though these three terms have the same general meaning, there is, nevertheless, great force in their very variety. For there is an implied contrast between washing and defilement — sanctification and pollution — justification and guilt. His meaning is, that having been once justified, they must not draw down upon themselves a new condemnation — that, having been sanctified, they must not pollute themselves anew — that, having been washed, they must not disgrace themselves with new defilements, but, on the contrary, aim at purity, persevere in true holiness, and abominate their former pollutions. And hence we infer what is the purpose for which God reconciles us to himself by the free pardon of our sins. While I have said that one thing is expressed by three terms, I do not mean that there is no difference whatever in their import, for, properly speaking, God justifies us when he frees us from condemnation, by not imputing to us our sins; he cleanses us, when he blots out the remembrance of our sins. Thus these two terms differ only in this respect, that the one is simple, while the other is figurative; for the term washing is metaphorical, Christ’s blood being likened to water. On the other hand, he sanctifies by renewing our depraved nature by his Spirit. Thus sanctification is connected with regeneration. In this passage, however, the Apostle had simply in view to extol, with many commendations, the grace of God, which has delivered us from the bondage of sin, that we may learn from this how much it becomes us to hold in abhorrence everything that stirs up against us God’s anger and vengeance.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, etc With propriety and elegance he distinguishes between different offices. For the blood of Christ is the procuring cause of our cleansing: righteousness and sanctification come to us through his death and resurrection. But, as the cleansing effected by Christ, and the attainment of righteousness, are of no avail except to those who have been made partakers of those blessings by the influence of the Holy Spirit, it is with propriety that he makes mention of the Spirit in connection with Christ. Christ, then, is the source of all blessings to us from him we obtain all things; but Christ himself, with all his blessings, is communicated to us by the Spirit. For it is by faith that we receive Christ, and have his graces applied to us. The Author of faith is the Spirit.
1 Corinthians 6:12-20
12. All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.
12. Omnium mihi est potestas, at non omnia conducunt: omnium mihi est potestas, sed ego sub nullius
“D’aucune chose, ou d’aucm;” — “Of anything, or of any one.”
redigar potestatem.
13. Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.
13. Escae ventri, et venter escis: Deus vero et has et ilium destruet. Corpus autem non scortationi, sed Domino, et Dominus corpori.
14. And God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.
14. Porro Deus et Dominum suscitavit, et nos suscitabit per potentiam suam.
15. Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid.
15. An nescitis, quod corpora vestra membra sunt Christi? tolthen lens igiturmembra Christi, faclam membra meretricis? Absit.
16. What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh.
16. An nescitis, quod qui adhaeret meretrici, unum corpus est? erunt enim, inquit, duo in carnem unam.
17. But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
17. Qui antera Domino adhaeret,unus spiritus est.
18. Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.
18. Fugite scortationem. Omne peccatum quod commiserit homo, extra corpus est: qui autem scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat.
19. What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
19. An nescitis, quod corpus vestrum templum est Spiritus sancti, qui in vobis est, quem habetis a Deo, et non estis vestri?
20. For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.
20. Empti enim estis pretio: glorificate iam Deum in corpore vestro et in spiritu vestro, quae Dei sunt.
entries.5d23540003c9dac7d4be5d647b07b7b4861e3eab: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.12" sID="gen118007" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">All things are lawful for me.</hi> Interpreters labor hard to make out the connection of these things, <note n="345"> <div sID="gen118009" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A le conioindre avec ce qui a este dit auparauant</foreign>;” — “To connect it with what has been said before.”<div eID="gen118009" type="x-p"/> </note> as they appear to be somewhat foreign to the Apostle’s design. For my own part, without mentioning the different interpretations, I shall state what, in my opinion, is the most satisfactory. It is probable, that the Corinthians even up to that time retained much of their former licentiousness, and had still a savor of the morals of their city. Now when vices stalk abroad with impunity, <note n="346"> <div sID="gen118010" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Or ou on peche a bride auallee, et la ou les vices ne sont point corrigez</foreign>;” — “Where persons sin with a loose bridle, and where vices are not punished.”<div eID="gen118010" type="x-p"/> </note> custom is regarded as law, and then afterwards vain pretexts are sought for by way of excuse; an instance of which we have in their resorting to the pretext of Christian liberty, so as to make almost everything allowable for themselves to do. They reveled in excess of luxury. With this there was, as usual, much pride mixed up. As it was an outward thing, they did not think that there was any sin involved in it: nay more, it appears from Paul’s words that they abused liberty so much as to extend it even to fornication. Now therefore, most appropriately, after having spoken of their vices, he discusses those base pretexts by which they flattered themselves in outward sins.<div eID="gen118008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118011" type="x-p"/>It is, indeed, certain, that he treats here of outward things, which God has left to the free choice of believers, but by making use of a term expressive of universality, he either indirectly reproves their unbridled licentiousness, or extols God’s boundless liberality, which is the best directress to us of moderation. For it is a token of excessive licentiousness, when persons do not, of their own accord, restrict themselves, and set bounds to themselves, amidst such manifold abundance. And in the <hi type="italic">first </hi>place, he limits liberty <note n="347"> <div sID="gen118012" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La liberte Chrestienne</foreign>;” — “Christian liberty.”<div eID="gen118012" type="x-p"/> </note> by two exceptions; and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, he warns them, that it does not by any means extend to fornication. These words, <hi type="italic">All things are lawful for me,</hi> must be understood as spoken in name of the Corinthians, <foreign xml:lang="el">κατ ᾿ ἀνθυποφορὰν,</foreign> (by anticipation,) as though he had said, I am aware of the reply which you are accustomed to make, when desirous to avoid reproof for outward vices. You pretend that <hi type="italic">all things are lawful</hi> for you, without any reserve or limitation.<div eID="gen118011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118013" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But all things are not expedient</hi> Here we have the <hi type="italic">first </hi>exception, by which he restricts the use of liberty — that they must not abandon themselves to licentiousness, because respect must be had to edification. <note n="348"> <div sID="gen118014" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’edification du prochain</foreign>;” — “The edification of their neighbor.”<div eID="gen118014" type="x-p"/> </note> The meaning is, “It is not enough that this or that is allowed us, to be made use of indiscriminately; for we must consider what is profitable to our brethren, whose edification it becomes us to study. For as he will afterwards point out at greater length, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.23 Bible:1Cor.10.24">1 Corinthians 10:23, 24</reference>,) and as he has already shown in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.13">Romans 14:13</reference>, etc., every one has liberty inwardly <note n="349"> <div sID="gen118015" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En sa conscience</foreign>;” — “In his conscience.”<div eID="gen118015" type="x-p"/> </note> in the sight of God on this condition, that all must restrict the use of their liberty with a view to mutual edification.<div eID="gen118013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118016" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">I will not be brought under the power of anything</hi> Here we have a <hi type="italic">second </hi>restriction — that we are constituted lords of all things, in such a way, that we ought not to bring ourselves under bondage to anything; as those do who cannot control their appetites. For I understand the word <foreign xml:lang="el">τινος </foreign>(any) to be in the neuter gender, and I take it as referring, not to persons, but to things, so that the meaning is this: “We are lords of all things; only we must not abuse that lordship in such a way as to drag out a most miserable bondage, being, through intemperance and inordinate lusts, under subjection to outward things, which ought to be under subjection to us.” And certainly, the excessive moroseness of those who grudge to yield up anything for the sake of their brethren, has this effect, that they unadvisedly put halters of necessity around their own necks.<div eID="gen118016" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118007" osisID="1Cor.6.12" type="section"/>
entries.e9884b766bdacba92fd91d2b6bf925e3f5269244: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.13" sID="gen118017" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats</hi> Here he shows what use ought to be made of outward things — for the necessity of the present life, which passes away quickly as a shadow, agreeably to what, he says afterwards. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.7.29">1 Corinthians 7:29</reference>.) <hi type="italic">We must use this world so as not to abuse it</hi> And hence, too, we infer, how improper it is for a Christian man to contend for outward things. <note n="350"> <div sID="gen118019" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il s’en fant que l’homme Chrestien se doyue soncier ne debatre pour les choses externes</foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">A </hi>Christian man ought not to be solicitous, or to contend for outward things.”<div eID="gen118019" type="x-p"/> </note> When a dispute, therefore, arises respecting corruptible things, a pious mind will not anxiously dwell upon these things; for liberty is one thing — the use of it is another. This statement accords with another — that<div eID="gen118018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118020" type="x-p"/>The kingdom of God is not meat and drink. <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.17">Romans 14:17</reference>.)<div eID="gen118020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118021" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Now the body is not for fornication</hi> Having mentioned the exceptions, he now states still farther, that our liberty ought not by any means to be extended to <hi type="italic">fornication</hi> For it was an evil that was so prevalent at that time, that it seemed in a manner as though it had been permitted; as we may see also from the decree of the Apostles, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.20">Acts 15:20</reference>,) where, in prohibiting the Gentiles from fornication, they place it among things indifferent; for there can be no doubt that this was done, because it was very generally looked upon as a lawful thing. Hence Paul says now, There is a difference between <hi type="italic">fornication </hi>and <hi type="italic">meats</hi>, for the Lord has not ordained <hi type="italic">the body for fornication</hi>, as he has <hi type="italic">the belly for meats</hi> And this he confirms from things contrary or opposite, inasmuch as it is consecrated to Christ, and it is impossible that Christ should be conjoined with fornication. What he adds — <hi type="italic">and the Lord for the body</hi>, is not without weight, for while God the Father has united us to his Son, what wickedness there would be in tearing away our body from that sacred connection, and giving it over to things unworthy of Christ. <note n="351"> <div sID="gen118022" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Choses du tout indignes de Christ</foreign>;” — “Things altogether unworthy of Christ.”<div eID="gen118022" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen118021" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118017" osisID="1Cor.6.13" type="section"/>
entries.cf1730da18954388208f6cb4cd390d9fc6fd2735: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.14" sID="gen118023" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi><hi type="italic"> And God hath also raised up the Lord</hi> He shows from Christ’s condition how unseemly fornication is for a Christian man; for Christ having been <hi type="italic">received </hi>into the heavenly glory, what has he in common with the pollutions of this world? <hi type="italic">Two </hi>things, however, <hi type="italic">are </hi>contained in these words. The <hi type="italic">first </hi>is, that it is unseemly and unlawful, that our body, which is consecrated to Christ, should be profaned by fornication, inasmuch as Christ himself has been raised up from the dead, that he might enter on the possession of the heavenly glory. The <hi type="italic">second </hi>is, that it is a base thing to prostitute our body <note n="352"> <div sID="gen118025" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est vne meschancete d’abandonner nostre corps, et le prostituer</foreign>;” — “It is wickedness to surrender our body, and prostitute it.”<div eID="gen118025" type="x-p"/> </note> to earthly pollutions, while it is destined to be a partaker <note n="353"> <div sID="gen118026" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Estre vn tour participant</foreign>;” — “To be one day a participant.”<div eID="gen118026" type="x-p"/> </note> along with Christ of a blessed immortality and of the heavenly glory. There is a similar statement in <reference osisRef="Bible:Col.3.1">Colossians 3:1</reference>, <hi type="italic">If we have risen with Christ</hi>, etc., with this difference, that he speaks here of the <hi type="italic">last </hi>resurrection only, while in that passage he speaks of the <hi type="italic">first </hi>also, or in other words, of the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which we are fashioned again to a new life. As, however, the resurrection is a thing almost <hi type="italic">incredible </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.8">Acts 26:8</reference>) to the human mind, when the Scripture makes mention of it, it reminds us of <hi type="italic">the power of God</hi>, with the view of confirming our faith in it. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.29">Matthew 22:29</reference>.)<div eID="gen118024" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118023" osisID="1Cor.6.14" type="section"/>
entries.1651797866373529487ac520439c8ec8355097ef: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.15" sID="gen118027" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">Know ye not that our bodies are the members</hi>, etc. Here we have an explanation, or, if you prefer it, an amplification of the foregoing statement. For that expression, <hi type="italic">the body is for the Lord</hi>, might, owing to its brevity, be somewhat obscure. Hence he says, as if with the view of explaining it, that Christ is joined with us and we with him in such a way, that we become one body with him. Accordingly, if I have connection with an harlot, I tear Christ in pieces, so far as it is in my power to do so; for it is impossible for me to draw Him into fellowship with such pollution. <note n="354"> <div sID="gen118029" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne pollution si fade et infame</foreign>;” — “A pollution so filthy and infamous.”<div eID="gen118029" type="x-p"/> </note> Now as that must be held in abhorrence, <note n="355"> <div sID="gen118030" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour ce que ceci est vne chose abominable, et que nous deuons auoir en horreur</foreign>;” — “As that is an abominable thing, and we must hold it in abhorrence.”<div eID="gen118030" type="x-p"/> </note> he makes use of the expression which he is accustomed to employ in reference to things that are absurd — <hi type="italic">God forbid</hi> <note n="356"> <div sID="gen118031" type="x-p"/> The original expression, <foreign xml:lang="el">Μή γέοιτο</foreign>!<hi type="italic"> Away with it</hi>! corresponds to the Hebrew term <foreign xml:lang="he">חללה</foreign>,<hi type="italic"> far be it</hi>! Thus in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.25">Genesis 18:25</reference>, <foreign xml:lang="he">חללה לך משת כדברהזה</foreign>,<hi type="italic"> Far be it from thee to act in this manner</hi>! Homer makes use of a similar expression — <foreign xml:lang="el">μὴ τοῦτο θεος τελεσειεν</foreign>, <hi type="italic">forbid that heaven should accomplish that</hi>! (Od. 20. 234.) — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen118031" type="x-p"/> </note> Observe, that the spiritual connection which we have with Christ belongs not merely to the soul, but also to the body, so that we are <hi type="italic">flesh of his flesh</hi>,<hi type="italic"> etc</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.30">Ephesians 5:30</reference>.) Otherwise the hope of a resurrection were weak, if our connection were not of that nature — full and complete.<div eID="gen118028" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118027" osisID="1Cor.6.15" type="section"/>
entries.ac8dd18035e36d53752cadb9d15d5e15580909b5: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.16" sID="gen118032" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">Know ye not that he that is joined to an harlot</hi> He brings out more fully the greatness of the injury that is done to Christ by the man that has intercourse with an harlot; for he becomes <hi type="italic">one body</hi>, and hence he tears away a member from Christ’s body. It is not certain in what sense he accommodates to his design the quotation which he subjoins from <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.24">Genesis 2:24</reference>. For if he quotes it to prove that two persons who commit fornication together become <hi type="italic">one flesh</hi>, he turns it aside from its true meaning to what is quite foreign to it. For Moses speaks there not of a base and prohibited cohabitation of a man and a woman, but of the marriage connection which God blesses. For he shows that that bond is so close and indissoluble, that it surpasses the relationship which subsists between a father and a son, which, assuredly, can have no reference to fornication. This consideration has led me sometimes to think, that this quotation is not brought forward to confirm the immediately preceding statement, but one that is more remote, in this way — “Moses says, that by the marriage connection husband and wife become <hi type="italic">one flesh</hi>, but <hi type="italic">he that is jointed to the Lord </hi>becomes not merely one flesh, but <hi type="italic">one spirit</hi> with him.” <note n="357"> <div sID="gen118034" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais nous sommes faits non seulement vne mesme chair auec le Seigneur, auquel nous adherons, mais aussi vn mesme esprit</foreign>;” — “But we have become not merely one flesh with the Lord, to whom we are joined, but also one spirit.”<div eID="gen118034" type="x-p"/> </note> And in this way the whole of this passage would tend to magnify the efficacy and dignity of the spiritual marriage which subsists between us and Christ.<div eID="gen118033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118035" type="x-p"/>If, however, any one does not altogether approve of this exposition, as being rather forced, I shall bring forward another. For as fornication is the corruption of a divine institution, it has some resemblance to it; and what is affirmed respecting the former, may to some extent be applied to the latter; not that it may be honored with the praises due to the former, <note n="358"> <div sID="gen118036" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Non que la paillardise soit digne de estre ornee des louanges qui appartienent a l’ordonnance du marriage</foreign>;” — “Not that fornication is worthy to be honored with the praises that belong to the ordinance of marriage.<div eID="gen118036" type="x-p"/> </note> but for the purpose of expressing the more fully the heinousness of the sin. The expression, therefore, that <hi type="italic">they two become one flesh</hi>, is applicable in the true and proper sense to married persons only; but it is applied to fornicators, who are joined in a polluted and impure fellowship, meaning that contagion passes from the one to the other. <note n="359"> <div sID="gen118037" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour monstrer que la contagion et vilenie passe de l’vn a l’autre</foreign>;” — “To show that contagion and pollution pass from the one to the other.”<div eID="gen118037" type="x-p"/> </note> For there is no absurdity in saying that fornication bears some resemblance to the sacred connection of marriage, as being a corruption of it, as I have said; but the former has a curse upon it, and the other a blessing. Such is the correspondence between things that are contrasted in an antithesis. At the same time, I would prefer to understand it, in the first instance, of marriage, and then, in an improper sense, <note n="360"> <div sID="gen118038" type="x-p"/> Our Author makes use of the adverb — <hi type="italic">abusive</hi>, (improperly,) referring, it is probable, to the figure of speech called by Quinctilian (8. 6) <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">abusio</hi></foreign> — the same as <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">catachresis</hi></foreign> (perversion.) — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen118038" type="x-p"/> </note> of fornication, in this way — “God pronounces husband and wife to be <hi type="italic">one flesh</hi>, in order that neither of them may have connection with another flesh; so that the adulterer and adulteress do, also, become <hi type="italic">one flesh</hi>, and involve themselves in an accursed connection. And certainly this is more simple, and agrees better with the context.<div eID="gen118035" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118032" osisID="1Cor.6.16" type="section"/>
entries.2ae8277e2254b68527e64b01a866bf868bc1bb8b: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.17" sID="gen118039" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is joined to the Lord.</hi> He has added this to show that our connection with Christ is closer than that of a husband and wife, and that the former, accordingly, must be greatly preferred before the latter, so that it must be maintained with the utmost chastity and fidelity. For if he who is joined to a woman in marriage ought not to have illicit connection with an harlot, much more heinous were this crime in believers, who are not merely <hi type="italic">one flesh</hi> with Christ, but also <hi type="italic">one spirit</hi> Thus there is a comparison between greater and less.<div eID="gen118040" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118039" osisID="1Cor.6.17" type="section"/>
entries.59c9275b6541776e1ae74125f0b3ac84821e4448: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.18" sID="gen118041" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">Flee fornication</hi> <hi type="italic">Every sin</hi>, etc. Having set before us honorable conduct, he now shows how much we ought to abhor <hi type="italic">fornication</hi>, setting before us the enormity of its wickedness and baseness. Now he shows its greatness by comparison — that this sin alone, of all sins, puts a brand of disgrace upon the body. The body, it is true, is defiled also by theft, and murder, and drunkenness, in accordance with those statements —<div eID="gen118042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118043" type="x-p"/>Your hands are defiled with blood. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.15">Isaiah 1:15</reference>.)<div eID="gen118043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118044" type="x-p"/>You have yielded your members instruments of iniquity unto sin, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.19">Romans 6:19</reference>,)<div eID="gen118044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118045" type="x-p"/>and the like. Hence some, in order to avoid this inconsistency, understand the words rendered <hi type="italic">against his own body</hi>, as meaning <hi type="italic">against us</hi>,<hi type="italic"> as being connected with Christ</hi>; but this appears to me to be more ingenious than solid. Besides, they do not escape even in this way, because that same thing, too, might be affirmed of idolatry equally with fornication. For he who prostrates himself before an idol, sins against connection with Christ. Hence I explain it in this way, that he does not altogether deny that there are other vices, in like manner, by which our body is dishonored and disgraced, but that his meaning is simply this — that defilement does not attach itself to our body from other vices in the same way <note n="361"> <div sID="gen118046" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">N’en demeure point tellement imprimee en nostre corps</foreign>;” — “Does not remain impressed upon our body in the same way.”<div eID="gen118046" type="x-p"/> </note> as it does from <hi type="italic">fornication</hi> My hand, it is true, is defiled by theft or murder, my tongue by evil speaking, or perjury, <note n="362"> <div sID="gen118047" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par mesdisance, detraction, et periure</foreign>;” — “By evil-speaking, detraction, and perjury.”<div eID="gen118047" type="x-p"/> </note> and the whole body by drunkenness; but <hi type="italic">fornication </hi>leaves a stain impressed upon the body, such as is not impressed upon it from other sins. According to this comparison, or, in other words, in the sense of less and more, other sins are said to be <hi type="italic">without the body</hi> — not, however, as though they do not at all affect the body, viewing each one by itself.<div eID="gen118045" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118041" osisID="1Cor.6.18" type="section"/>
entries.62aa63d7089ad2af9169c4a2e6117334a7c42edf: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.6.19" sID="gen118048" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">Know ye not that your body</hi> He makes use of two additional arguments, in order to deter us from this filthiness. <hi type="italic">First</hi>, That <hi type="italic">our bodies are temples of the Spirit</hi>; and, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, that <hi type="italic">the Lord has bought us to himself as his property.</hi> There is an emphasis implied in the term <hi type="italic">temple</hi>; for as the Spirit of God cannot take up his abode in a place that is profane, we do not give him a habitation otherwise than by consecrating ourselves to him as <hi type="italic">temples</hi> It is a great honor that God confers upon us when he <hi type="italic">desires to dwell </hi>in us. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.14">Psalm 132:14</reference>.) Hence we ought so much the more to fear, lest he should depart from us, offended by our sacrilegious actings. <note n="363"> <div sID="gen118050" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par nos vilenies plenes de sacrilege</foreign>;” — “By our defilements, full of sacrilege.”<div eID="gen118050" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen118049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118051" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And ye are not your own.</hi> Here we have a <hi type="italic">second </hi>argument — that we are not at our own disposal, that we should live according to our own pleasure. He proves this from the fact that the Lord has purchased us for himself, by paying the price of our redemption. There is a similar statement in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.9">Romans 14:9</reference><div eID="gen118051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118052" type="x-p"/>To this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord of the living and the dead.<div eID="gen118052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118053" type="x-p"/>Now the word rendered <hi type="italic">price </hi>may be taken in two ways; either simply, as we commonly say of anything that it has cost a price, <note n="364"> <div sID="gen118054" type="x-p"/> Thus, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐξευρίσκειν</foreign>, is employed by classical writers to mean — getting a thing <hi type="italic">at a price</hi>, that is, at a high price. See Herod. 7. 119. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen118054" type="x-p"/> </note> when we mean that it has not been got for nothing; or, as used instead of the adverb <foreign xml:lang="el">τιμίως</foreign> <hi type="italic">at a dear rate</hi>, as we are accustomed to say of things that have cost us much. This latter view pleases me better. In the same way Peter says,<div eID="gen118053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118055" type="x-p"/>Ye are redeemed, not with gold and silver, but with the precious <note n="365"> <div sID="gen118056" type="x-p"/> Our Author has very manifestly in his eye the epithet <foreign xml:lang="el">τιμίος</foreign>, (precious,) as made use of by the Apostle Peter, in reference to the blood of Christ — <foreign xml:lang="el">τιμίῳ αἱματι, ὡς ἀμνου ἀμώμου κ. τ. λ.</foreign> — “precious blood, as of a Lamb without blemish,” etc. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen118056" type="x-p"/> </note> blood of the Lamb, without spot. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.18 Bible:1Pet.1.19">1 Peter 1:18,19</reference>.)<div eID="gen118055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118057" type="x-p"/>The sum is this, <note n="366"> <div sID="gen118058" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le sommaire et la substance du propos revient la</foreign>;” — “The sum and substance of the discourse amount to this.”<div eID="gen118058" type="x-p"/> </note> that redemption must hold us bound, and with a bridle of obedience restrain the lasciviousness of our flesh.<div eID="gen118057" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.6.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118048" osisID="1Cor.6.19" type="section"/>

20. Glorify God From this conclusion, it appears that the Corinthians took a liberty to themselves in outward things, that it was necessary to restrain and bridle. The reproof therefore is this he allows that the body is subject to God no less than the soul, and that accordingly it is reasonable that both be devoted to his glory. “As it is befitting that the mind of a believer should be pure, so there must be a corresponding outward profession also before men, inasmuch as the power of both is in the hands of God, who has redeemed both.” With the same view he declared a little ago, that not only our souls but our bodies also are temples of the Holy Spirit, that we may not think that we discharge our duty to him aright, if we do not devote ourselves wholly and entirely to his service, that he may by his word regulate even the outward actions of our life.
CHAPTER 7
1 Corinthians 7:1-2
1. Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.
1. Porro, de quibus scripsistis mihi, bonum est viro mulierem non tangere.
2. Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.
2. Propter fornicationes autem unusquisque uxorem suam habeat, et unaquaeque proprium maritum.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="6" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. VI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 DAre any of you having a matter against ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, go to law before the unjust, and not before the Saints? <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle having already sharply reflected upon this Church for their <ns0:hi>Pride,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Contentions,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Divisions</ns0:hi> (which were branches from that root) and for their <ns0:hi>vili<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ying</ns0:hi> him who was their spiritual Father, and magnifying their Instructors a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove him, as also for their loosness in their Church-discipline; he cometh in this Chapter to another thing, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> their going to Law before <ns0:hi>Pagan Iudges</ns0:hi>; for such was the misery of those times, that they had no other, though some think that they might have had (the Pagan persecutions being as yet not be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gun.) The Apostle speaks of this as a thing which he wondred that they durst be guilty of, that they should be no more ten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der of the glory of God in the reputation of the Christian Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligion, and should not rather chuse Arbitrators amongst the Members of their Church, to hear and determine such diffe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rences as arose amongst them, than give <ns0:hi>Pagans</ns0:hi> an occasion to reproach the Christian Religion for the contentions and feuds of Christians. The reputation of the Gospel and the Professors of it, being the thing for which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was here concerned, and upon the account of which he thus speaketh: it becometh Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians yet to consider, whether what he saith concerneth not them, where either the Judges or the generality of the Auditors in such Judgments, may probably reproach Religion, or that way of God which they owne, for their trivial and uncharitable contentions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Do ye not know that the Saints shall judge the world <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If indeed the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> had had no other competent Judges, they had been to have been excused, in making use of Infidel Judges; but (saith the Apostle) you have other persons competent enough, whom you may (by your submission to them) make Judges; for <ns0:hi>you know that the Saints shall judge the world.</ns0:hi> In the same sense (as some think) as Christ saith the <ns0:hi>Ninevites</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Queen of the South</ns0:hi> should rise up in judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment against the Jews, and condemn them; but certainly there is something more than that in it, when the Apostle said, <ns0:hi>The Saints should judge the world,</ns0:hi> he intended to say something of them, which was not common to some Heathens with them. Others therefore think, that the Saints in the day of Judgment shall judge the World, approving the Sentence of Christ pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounced against the World, and as being Assessors with Christ, which indeed is what Christ said of the Apostles, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 19.28. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.30. Others think, that the phrase only signifieth a great honour and dignity, to which the Saints shall be advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ced. A late learned and very <ns0:hi>Critical Author</ns0:hi> hath another no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the Saints <ns0:hi>judging the world</ns0:hi> here spoken of, interpret<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing it of a time when the <ns0:hi>secular<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Iudgment</ns0:hi> of the World should be given to the <ns0:hi>Saints,</ns0:hi> which was prophesied by <ns0:hi>Daniel, ch.</ns0:hi> 7.18, 27. and therefore might be known by them, if this be the sense. It is either a Prophecy of Gods giving the Government of the World into the hands of Christians, (which fell out after this in <ns0:hi>Constantines</ns0:hi> time) or else it signifies such a time towards the end of the World, as those that expect a <ns0:hi>fifth Monarchy</ns0:hi> speak of, when those that are <ns0:hi>true Saints,</ns0:hi> in the strictest sense, shall have the Government of the World, which seemeth not probable, considering what the Scripture speaks of persecutions, and wars, and disorders, rather increasing, than abating to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards the End of the World. The Apostle therefore here seemeth rather to speak of the Saints judging the World in the last day, approving the Sentence of Christ the Judge of the quick and the dead; or else to prophesie of that time, when Christianity should so far obtain in the World, that the Govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment either of the whole World, or of a great part of it, should be in the hands of Christians.</ns0:note>? And if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters? <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">From whence the Apostle strongly concludeth the competency of Christians to arbitrate and determine little matters of difference amongst Christians, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n their commerce and civil dealings one with another.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:441" />3 Know ye not that we shall judge Angels <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That the Saints shall judge Angels, is here so plainly assert<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, as a thing within their knowledge, that none can doubt <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t; but how, or when, or what Angels, is not so easily deter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mined. The best Interpreters understand it of the <ns0:hi>evil Angels,</ns0:hi> that is, the Devils, whom the Saints shall judge at the last day, agreeing with the Judge of the whole Earth in the Sentence, which he shall then give against the <ns0:hi>evil Angels,</ns0:hi> confining them to the bottomless Pit, who while this World lasteth, have a greater liberty as <ns0:hi>Princes of the Air,</ns0:hi> to rove abroad in the Air, and to work mightily in the children of disobedience. Others understand the <ns0:hi>judging of Angels</ns0:hi> here mentioned, of the spoil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Devils of the Kingdom that they exercise in the World, in the places where the Gospel hath not prevailed, by <ns0:hi>lying Oracles,</ns0:hi> and seducing men to Idolatry, and the worship<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ping of Devils: in which sense Christ said, <ns0:hi>Now shall the Prince of this world be cast out,</ns0:hi> Joh. 12.31.</ns0:note>? how much more things that pertain to this life? <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">From hence the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle argues the competency of their brethren to judge of, and to determine those little matters which were in difference be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt them, being but things concerning this life, being of far less consequence than the judging of the World and the Evil Angels at the last day.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 If then ye have judgment of things pertaining to this life <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That is, if you have any cause of suing, or impleading one another for things that pertain to this life, be they of what na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture they will.</ns0:note>, set them to judge who are least estee<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med in the Church <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">rather commit the umpirage and determi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation of such little differences to the meanest Members of your Church, than go to contend before <ns0:hi>Pagans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Infidels:</ns0:hi> or do not imploy your Teachers about them, who have higher work to be imployed in; but imploy those who are of a lower order in the Church, and whose business and concerns lye in secular affairs.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 I speak to your shame. <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">I do not speak this, as if I would have you make choice of the meanest persons among you to arbitrate and determine all matters that may be in difference betwixt you, but it would be a shame to you.</ns0:note> Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? no not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But brother goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">If amongst you all there could not be found one man whom you can judge wise enough to determine differences betwixt you about things of this life, without bringing one another into Pagan Courts, to the reproach and scandal of the Religion which you profess, make use of any, yea, the meanest Christians in such Judgments, rather than Infidels and Unbelievers, who will make use of your differences, to the reproaching of the holy Name of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Not that it is simply unlawful for men to make use of hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mane Laws, and Courts, and methods of Judicature; for even the Laws of men are good, if they be lawfully used: and the word here used by the Apostle is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which signifieth ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther an impotency or weakness of mind and affections, a defect or diminution from perfection, than any scandalous sin. Going to Law with brethren (though lawful in it self) may be made unlawful by circumstances: 1. When it is before Judges that are Unbelievers, so as mens going to Law before them, tends to the reproach of Religion, the credit and reputation of the Gospel ought to be dearer to us than any little secular concern. This was the case in this place. 2. When it is for little mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters, such as a <ns0:hi>Coat</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>Cloak</ns0:hi> It is against the Law of Charity to do another a great wrong to recover to our selves a little that is our right. 3. When we cannot do it without <ns0:hi>wrath, anger, impatience, covetousness,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>desire of revenge.</ns0:hi> It is a thing possi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to go to Law without sin, but what very few do, through that corruption which cleaveth to corrupt Nature.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.17<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 1 Thess. 5.15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> why do ye not rather take wrong <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is therefore far more becoming conscientious Christians to take a little wrong,</ns0:note>? why do ye not rather suffer your selves to be defrauded? <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">and to suffer themselves to be cheated of their right, especially under such circumstances, where the credit of the Gospel and Religion must lose more than they can get. And to do otherwise speaks <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, a defect or imperfection in Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians, and is not without its guilt. If by their contentiousness, they do not shew themselves so bad, as some would make them who hold all contendings at Law amongst Christians unlawful, yet they do not shew themselves so good as the Rule of Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stianity requireth them to be, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 5.39, 40. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 6.29. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.19.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Nay, you do wrong and defraud, and that <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> brethren <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Apostle riseth higher in his charge against them, he had before only charged them for want of self-denial, that they could not bear or suffer wrong; he now chargeth them for doing wrong and defrauding, and that not Heathens (which yet had been bad enough) but Christians that were their brethren, whom they had the highest obligations upon them imaginable to love, and to do good to. And indeed this charge followeth di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rectly upon the other: For as in War, one Army always are mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derers, or guilty of the blood which they spill; so in suing at Law (which is a Civil War betwixt the two Parties) either the one or the other Party suing must do wrong, either putting his brother to trouble and expence, to recover of him what is not his right, or that he might withhold from him what is truly and indeed his right, either of which is indeed a doing of wrong or defrauding.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Know ye not <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Thess. 4.6.</ns0:note> that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That by the Kingdom of God is here meant the Kingdom of Glory, the happiness of another life, is plain, because he speaketh in the Future tense; this Kingdom, he saith, the <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />righteous,</ns0:hi> that is, those who so live and dye, shall not inherit. If we take the term <ns0:hi>Vnrighteous</ns0:hi> here to be a generical term, the <ns0:hi>Species,</ns0:hi> or some of the principal <ns0:hi>Species,</ns0:hi> of which are after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards enumerated, it signifieth here the same with notoriously wicked men. But if we take it to signifie persons guilty of acts of injustice towards themselves or others, it cannot be here un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood as a general term, relating to all those <ns0:hi>Species</ns0:hi> of Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners after enumerated; for so <ns0:hi>Idolaters</ns0:hi> cannot properly be cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led Unrighteous, but Ungodly men.</ns0:note>? Be not deceived <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Be not deceived</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) either by any false Teachers, or by the many ill examples of such sinners that you daily have, nor by Magistrates connivence at these sins.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 15.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>0. Gal. 5.21. Eph. 5.5. 1 Tim. 1.9. Heb. 12.14. Rev. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>2.15.</ns0:note> neither fornicators <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Neither such as being single per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons commit uncleanness with others (for here the Apostle di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stinguisheth these sinners from Adulterers, whom he mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth afterward.)</ns0:note>, nor idolaters <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Nor such as either worship the Creature in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stead of God, or worship the true God before Images.</ns0:note>, nor adul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terers <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Nor such as being married persons break their Marriage-cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant, and commit uncleanness with such as are not their yoke-fellows.</ns0:note>, nor effeminate persons <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Nor persons that give up themselves to lascivious<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, burning continually in lusts.</ns0:note>, nor abusers of themselves with mankind <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Nor such as are guilty of the sin of <ns0:hi>Sodom,</ns0:hi> a sin not to be named amongst Christians or men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Nor thieves <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Nor such as take away the goods of their neighbours clan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />destinely, or by violence, without their consent or any just au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thority.</ns0:note>, nor covetous <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Nor persons who discover themselves excessively to love money, by their endeavours to get it into their hands any way, by oppression, cheating, or defrauding others.</ns0:note>, nor drunk<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ards <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Nor persons that make drinking their business, and use it excessive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, without regard to the Law and Rules of Temperance and Sobriety.</ns0:note>, nor revilers <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Nor persons that use their tongues intemperately, ralling at others, and reviling them with reproachful and op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />probrious names.</ns0:note>, nor extortioners <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Nor any such as by violence wring out of peoples hands what is not their due. None of these not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />penting of these sinful courses, and turning from them into a contrary course of life, shall ever come in Heaven.</ns0:note>, shall in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />herit the kingdom of God.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap>. 10.12.</ns0:note> some of you <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In the two last verses the Apostle had pronounced a ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rible Sentence, especially to the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> who having been Heathens lately, had wallowed in a great deal of this guilt; he therefore here, that they might be humbled, and have low thoughts of themselves, and not puffed up (as he had before charged them) mindeth them, that some of them had been guilty of some of these enormous sins, some of them of one, or some of them, and others of other of them.</ns0:note>: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">But that they might not despair in their reflections upon that guilt, he tells them, <ns0:hi>they were washed,</ns0:hi> not only with the <ns0:hi>Baptism of water,</ns0:hi> but with the <ns0:hi>Baptism of the blood of Christ,</ns0:hi> and with the <ns0:hi>Baptism of the Holy Ghost,</ns0:hi> born again of <ns0:hi>Water and of the Spirit,</ns0:hi> Joh. 3.5. yea, and not only <ns0:hi>washed,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>sanctified,</ns0:hi> filled with new, spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual habits, through the <ns0:hi>renewing of the Holy Ghost.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but ye are <ns0:note place="margin">

                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 10.12.</ns0:note> justified in the Name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Having obtained a true righteousness, in which they might stand and appear before God, even the Righteousness of Christ reckoned unto them for righteousness, <ns0:hi>justified</ns0:hi> through the Merits of the Lord Jesus Christ, and <ns0:hi>sanctified</ns0:hi> through the Spirit of Holiness: So that the washing first mentioned in this verse, seemeth to be a generical term, comprehending both <ns0:hi>Iustification,</ns0:hi> remission of sin, and deliverance from the guilt of it, and also <ns0:hi>Regenera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sanctification,</ns0:hi> which is the proper effect of the Spirit of Grace, creating in the Soul new habits and dispositions, by which it is inabled and inclined, as to dye unto sin, so to live un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to God. This the Apostle doth not say of them all, (for it is very probable there were in this Church some Hypocrites) but of some of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.23.</ns0:note> All things are lawful unto me <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The words of this Text are not so difficult in themselves, as it is to make out the connexion they have with, and the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pendence they have upon what went before, and what follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth after. Some thinking that they refer unto what the Apostle had said before about their going to Law before Infidels in the seven first verses, lest any should say, Is it not then lawful for men to sue at Law for their just dues and rights? The Apostle answers, Admit it be, yet Christians ought not only to consider what is strictly lawful and just, but they ought to consider cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances; for, <ns0:hi>Quicquid non expedit,</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>quantum non expedit non licet,</ns0:hi> is an old and good Rule; An action that is in it self lawful, may be by circumstances made sinful and unlawful; and that was the case as to the Christians going to Law before Infidels. But others, and those the most, think that the Apostle here begins a new head of discourse to disswade from the sin of fornication, and from an intemperate use of <ns0:hi>meat</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>drink,</ns0:hi> as being pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vocative of lust, and disposing them to that sin. Now lest they should say, Is it not lawful then to <ns0:hi>eat</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>drink</ns0:hi> liberally, must we eat and drink for bare necessity? He answereth, <ns0:hi>All things are lawful for me,</ns0:hi> that is, all things which are not for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bidden by the Law of God may be used, may be done, under fair circumstances; but circumstances may alter the case,</ns0:note>, but all things are not <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>profitable.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> expedient <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">all things may not be expedient to be used, or done by all persons, or at all times. The <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> might possibly conclude too much from what he had told them, that they were <ns0:hi>washed, ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stified,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>sanctified, viz.</ns0:hi> that now all things were <ns0:hi>lawful</ns0:hi> to them, at least all things, not simply and absolutely condemned in the Word of God, the Apostle correcteth their mistake, by telling them they were to have a regard to expedience, and the profit of others, the neglect of which might make things that were in themselves lawful to become unlawful.</ns0:note>: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Besides, that they must take heed, that they did not make such an use, even of lawful things, as to be brought under the power of them, which men are, when they become potent temptations to them to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>in against God any way.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap> 14.17.</ns0:note> Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The beginning of this verse seemeth to give a great light to our true understanding of the former verse, and maketh it ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry probable, that the Apostle spake with reference to the free use of meats and drinks, when he said, <ns0:hi>All things are lawful for me.</ns0:hi> Though God hath ordained meats for the filling of the belly, and hath made the belly for the receptacle of meats, for the nourishment of the body, so as the use of meats and drinks is lawf<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>l, yet when we see that the free use of them pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth inexpedient, as too much pampering the body, and dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posing it to wantonness, so far as they do so, they are to be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voided. Others make the connexion thus, all your contests are but for things which concern the belly, for meats and drinks, for perishing things: now in things of this nature, all things that are lawful are not expedient. Others say, That the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle here answereth or obviateth what the <ns0:hi>Nicolaitans</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Epicureans</ns0:hi> held, That all sorts of meats and drinks were lawful, yea, <ns0:hi>fornication it self.</ns0:hi> The Apostle grants the first, but deni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the second, there being not a parity of reason for the law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness of meats, and drinks, and of fornication.</ns0:note>: but God shall destroy both it and them <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He tells them, God had ordained meats for the belly of man, and had created the <ns0:hi>stomach</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>belly</ns0:hi> for the reception of meats for the nourish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of mans body, and the preservation of his life; yet they ought to use them lawfully, and to consider expedience in the use of them, and not too eagerly to contend for them, for God shall destroy both the belly, and the use of meats as to the belly. In the Resurrection, as men shall not marry, nor give in marri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />age, so they shall hunger and thirst no more.</ns0:note>.                   </ns0:gap> members of Christ <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Christ is united to the person of the Believer, and he is the Head of the Church, which is his mystical Body; so that the bodies of Believers are in a sense the Members of Christ, and should be used by us as the Members of Christ, which we should not rend from him: but</ns0:note>? Shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an har<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lot <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">he that doth commit fornication, rends his body from Christ, and maketh it the member of an Harlot; for as the man and wife are one flesh by Divine ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2.24. so the Fornicator and the Harlot are one flesh by an impure conjunction.</ns0:note>? Eph. 4.4. & 5.30.</ns0:note> is one spirit <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This phrase <ns0:hi>joyned to the Lord,</ns0:hi> is thought to be taken out of <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 10.20. <ns0:hi>To him thou shalt cleave.</ns0:hi> He that hath attained to that mystical Union which is betwixt Christ and every one that is a true Believer, is not essentially, but spiritually and my<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stically <ns0:hi>one Spirit</ns0:hi> with Christ, his spirit is united to the Spirit of Christ, and he is one by him in Faith and love, and by obedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence, Christ and he have one will, and he is ruled and govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by Christ: therefore you must take heed what you do in making your bodies the members of Harlots, which they can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not be, and the Members of Christ also.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Flee fornication: Every sin that a man doth, is without the body <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Apostle cometh to a new Argument, by which he presseth them to f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ee the sin of Uncleanness. It is observed by some, that this sin is peculiarly to be resisted, not so much by resisting it, and pondering arguments against it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as by flying from it, avoiding all occasions of it, and not suffering our thoughts to feed upon it; but the Apostles argument is, because other sins are <ns0:hi>without the body,</ns0:hi> that is, the body hath not such a <ns0:hi>blemish</ns0:hi> and note or mark of infamy laid upon it by any other sin as by this: in drunkenness the <ns0:hi>liquor,</ns0:hi> in gluttony the <ns0:hi>meat</ns0:hi>; in other sins, something without a mans self is that which is a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bused, but the <ns0:hi>body it self</ns0:hi> is the thing which is abused in this filthy sin.</ns0:note>: but he that committeth for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nication, sinneth against his own body <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">So he that is guilty of it, sinneth not only against his wife, with whom he is one flesh, but against his body, which he abuseth in this vile and sinful act, and upon which he im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prints a mark of infamy and disgrace, a blot not to be washed out but with the blood of Christ. So as though by other sins men may sin against their own bodies, yet by no sin so eminently as by this sin. Other sins have their seat in the mind and soul, the body, and commonly some particular member of the body, is but the servant of the Soul in the execution and commit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ing of them, Lust, though indeed it ariseth from the heart, yet it is committed more in the body, than any other sin is.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:442" />19 What, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 6.16.</ns0:note> know ye not that your body is the temple of the holy Ghost, <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> in you <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The Apostle, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 3.16. had called the Church of <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinth,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> of God, and there made use of it, to disswade them from dissensions and divisions, because by them they de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filed and destroyed the Temple of God; here he calls the Members of that Church, the <ns0:hi>Temple of the Holy Ghost,</ns0:hi> which strongly proveth the Holy Ghost to be God. He makes use of it here as an Argument to disswade them from the sin of forni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation. Gods Temple was builded for his <ns0:hi>habitation</ns0:hi> upon Earth, the place which he chose most to manifest himself in to his people, and for a place wherein his people were to pay him that external Homage and Worship, which he required of them under the Law. So as the Apostles calling them the Temple of the Holy Ghost, both minded them of the favour God had bestowed on them, and also of that homage and duty, which they with their bodies were to pay unto God: the latter they could not perform, nor hope for the former, while they lived in the practice of a sin so contrary to the Will of God.</ns0:note>, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sides, he mindeth them, that their bodies were not their own, they had them of God: they had them from God by Creation, and they were upheld by the daily workings of his Providence in their upholding and preservation; God had not given them their bodies for this use, the body was not <ns0:hi>for fornication,</ns0:hi> as he had told them, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. So as in abusing their bodies, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> abused what was not their own, nor in their own power <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> use, as they listed to use them; but to be used only for those ends, and in that manner, that he who had given them, had prescribed and directed, and in these abuses there was a kind of Sacriledge. As God of old charged the Jews, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16.17, 18, 19, 20. that they had taken the <ns0:hi>Iewels</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>his gold and his silver,</ns0:hi> to make Images, and commit spiritual Whoredom with them, and they had taken his <ns0:hi>meat,</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>fine flour,</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>oyl,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cense</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>set before them,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.23. Heb. 9.12.</ns0:note> For ye are bought with a price <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">What price this is that is here mentioned, <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> tells us both <ns0:hi>Negatively</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Positively,</ns0:hi> 1 Pet. 1.18, 19. <ns0:hi>Forasmuch as ye know that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers: But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb, without blemish and without spot.</ns0:hi> So he argueth with them against this sin from their <ns0:hi>Redemption,</ns0:hi> it being suitable to rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, that those who are redeemed out of any slavery or capti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vity, should be the servants of him who redeemed them, not of those Tyrants from whom they are redeemed, such are our lusts and corruptions, from which we are redeemed, as well as from that curse and wrath, which is the consequent of them.</ns0:note>: there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore glorifie God in your body, and in your spirit, which are Gods <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Therefore (saith the Apostle) you who are redeemed with a price, and with such a price are bound to <ns0:hi>glorifie God,</ns0:hi> as by speaking well of his Name, so by obeying his Will, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 5.16. And this you are bound to do, not with your bodies or spirits only, but in or with your bodies and spirits also, that is, with your whole man; for both of them <ns0:hi>are Gods,</ns0:hi> by a mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fold right, not that of Creation and Providence only, but that of Redemption also: with which exhortation the Apostle finish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth this discourse, and cometh to give them an answer to some questions about which they had wrote unto him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
